grounds.point: Section 14(1)(b) requires a post-9 June 1952 subletting, assignment or other parting with possession without the landlord's written consent.
grounds.explanation: The supplied statutory text expressly makes subletting, assignment or other parting with possession after 9 June 1952, without written landlord consent, the conditions of the fixed eviction ground.

grounds.point: M.L. Sharma occupied part of the premises in connection with his employment with the insurance company.
grounds.explanation: Respondents 2-4 stated that Sharma had been an employee and was given accommodation because of that employment, while respondent witnesses identified employment records and RW3 testified that he worked as a driver for New Zealand Insurance Company and continued with National Insurance Company. This supports an employment-linked origin of his occupation, although it does not itself resolve whether possession was later parted with for purposes of section 14(1)(b).

grounds.point: M.L. Sharma continued residing at the premises after his employment had ended.
grounds.explanation: Respondents 2-4 stated that after Sharma's retirement in 1978 the company never required him to vacate, RW2 did not know whether he was expressly allowed to remain after retirement, and RW3 confirmed that Sharma was not employed in 1998-1999 and later died at 40/16. Continued residence is therefore supported, but the record does not by that fact alone establish the legally required parting with possession.

grounds.point: National Insurance Company parted with possession of the relevant portion to M.L. Sharma.
grounds.explanation: The petitioner alleged Sharma's exclusive possession, while respondent No.1 denied any subletting, assignment or parting and asserted possession of the premises in its entirety. The evidence establishes Sharma's residence, including after employment, but supplies no resolving finding or evidence concerning whether the tenant retained legal or practical possession and control; the reported Parasaram discussion confirms the breadth of section 14(1)(b) but concerns a different liquidation-sale setting and does not resolve that factual issue here.

grounds.point: Roop Sharma and Rajiv Nanda were in exclusive possession of part of the tenanted premises through a transfer from respondent No.1.
grounds.explanation: The petitioner alleged exclusive possession by Roop Sharma and Rajiv Nanda, but respondents 2-4 said they were respectively Sharma's son and son-in-law, were not permanent occupants and merely visited him; RW3 corroborated the family relationships. The allowed record contains no resolving finding or other evidence establishing that respondent No.1 transferred possession to either of them.

grounds.point: Any qualifying subletting, assignment or parting with possession occurred without the landlord's written consent.
grounds.explanation: The petitioner repeatedly alleged absence of written consent, while respondents 2-4 denied that the premises had been given to them without written consent. No written consent, notice of sub-tenancy, or resolving finding on consent appears in the allowed record, so this statutory condition cannot be treated as established or disproved.

grounds.point: The supplied precedent material gives section 14(1)(b) a broad reach encompassing assignment and other modes of parting with possession.
grounds.explanation: General Radio reports Parasaram as holding that Delhi section 14(b) is broad enough to include sublease, assignment and other modes of parting with possession, including an involuntary sale. Telesound expressed only a prima facie view concerning amalgamation and expressly reserved the section 14(1)(b) eviction issue, while General Radio's direct application arose under the Andhra Pradesh statute; none supplies a decisive rule that Sharma's continued post-employment residence on this record necessarily constituted parting with possession.

reason: The allowed record supports Sharma's employment-linked occupation and his continued residence after employment, but it does not resolve whether respondent No.1 actually parted with possession, whether Roop Sharma or Rajiv Nanda received possession, or whether any qualifying transfer lacked written consent. Because those conditions are material under the supplied section 14(1)(b) and the supplied precedent does not close the factual and legal gaps for this employee-accommodation setting, the fixed eviction ground remains undetermined.
